title: Atomoxetine-associated Raynaud’s phenomenon in children: an under-recognized risk of non-stimulant ADHD therapy
authors: Wenxiu Mo, Lin Liu, Zheyu Cui, Yan Li, Huawei Mao
abstract: Raynaud’s phenomenon (RP) is an increasingly recognized yet still underreported adverse effect of ADHD pharmacotherapy. Whereas stimulant-associated RP is well documented, atomoxetine-related RP has surfaced only in isolated pediatric cases, leaving a gap in our understanding of non-stimulant toxicity. This narrative review reports the first Asian pediatric case identified in English- and regional-language literature and synthesizes the global evidence base, integrating five pediatric cases, targeted literature retrieval, and disproportionality analyses of FAERS and WHO VigiBase. Atomoxetine carries a consistent pharmacovigilance signal for RP. Beyond the elevation of synaptic cleft norepinephrine, the five cases point to suspected contributors: plasma drug concentration, CYP2D6-mediated metabolic variability—particularly relevant in East Asian populations—and individual susceptibility with superimposed triggers. Onset latency is highly variable (hours to years), and the course in reported cases is milder and fully reversible, without digital ulceration, features consistent with, though not determined by, the sustained, gradual peripheral noradrenergic elevation produced by selective norepinephrine transporter inhibition, in contrast to the rapid catecholamine surges typical of stimulants. These findings call for longitudinal vigilance beyond the titration phase, prompt exclusion of secondary causes, and systematic pharmacovigilance reporting.

title: Artificial intelligence diffusion, adaptive Human-Capital Transformation, and unequal development: evidence from a 50-country panel
authors: Gustavo Pessoa, Svetlana Tolstikova, Nurlan Kaldibayev, Zhanneta Gerzelieva, Vadim Ponkratov, Andrey Masterov, Nikolay Kuznetsov, Andrey Pozdnyaev, Elena Mikhina, Anna Shkalenko, Marina Vasiljeva, Irina Nikolaeva
abstract: Introduction Despite expanding artificial intelligence (AI) research, evidence remains fragmented on how AI capacity, Human-Capital Transformation, institutions, and labor-market structure jointly relate to unequal development. Methods Using 229 country-year observations from 50 purposively selected economies over 2020–2024, this study integrates conceptual development, composite measurement, panel estimation, country configurations, and conditional projections for 2026–2027. Moving beyond traditional productivist paradigms, this study conceptualizes adaptive human capital (AHC) as the dynamic capacity to preserve, renew, recombine, and redeploy human capabilities under technological change, with health sustaining adaptability, lifelong learning enabling renewal, and skills recalibration supporting resilience. This model distinguishes adaptive capacity from its observable educational and digital foundations. Five author-constructed indices capture AI Diffusion Capacity (AIDC), Human-Capital Transformation (HCT), Enabling Conditions, AI-Related Labor-Market Pressure, and multidimensional Development Outcomes. Two-way fixed-effects models use country-clustered standard errors, restricted wild-cluster-bootstrap inference, and false-discovery-rate correction. Sensitivity checks examine alternative weights, component exclusion, and 1,000 positive random-weight draws. Results AIDC coefficients are positive for HCT (β = 0.220, p = 0.0063) and Development Outcomes (β = 0.160, p = 0.027), although the latter attenuates after income adjustment. The strongest results concern labor absorption: negative AIDC coefficients for total unemployment (β = −0.359) and youth unemployment (β = −0.319) and a positive coefficient for the employment-to-population ratio (β = 0.258) remain significant after income adjustment and false-discovery-rate correction. Comparisons among similar AIDC countries identify configuration-level heterogeneity without a consistently dominant human-capital, institutional, or labor-market correlate. Complementary AIDC–HCT and AIDC–unemployment maps distinguish aligned and asymmetric country configurations; the latter classifies 14, 12, 11, and 13 economies into four labor-market groups. Conditional joint AIDC–HCT paths imply declining Development Outcomes under the lower scenario and improving outcomes under the central and upper scenarios; separate AIDC paths map labor-configuration transitions. Discussion Unequal development is reflected in asymmetric technological and labor-market configurations: 12 countries combine above-average AIDC with above-median unemployment, whereas 11 combine below-average AIDC with unemployment at or below the sample median of 4.545%. The study connects an adaptive human-capital framework with differentiated empirical evidence on technological capacity, human capabilities, and labor absorption, informing country-specific priorities for technological scaling, capability renewal, and support during labor-market transitions.

title: Scaffolding young children’s AI use: opening pedagogical black boxes in early childhood classrooms
authors: Xinyun Hu, Boris Wai Yan Choy
abstract: Abstract Given their real-time responsive capabilities, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have been positioned as cognitive partners for young children. However, research and policy directives have tended toward technological determinism, which black-boxes how these technologies function in early childhood education (ECE). Applying Actor-Network Theory (ANT), this qualitative case study deconstructs pedagogical black boxes during a plant inquiry unit involving a teacher, four children (aged 5–6), and AI-integrated devices. The findings provide a typology of three pedagogical black boxes: operational (obscuring technical constraints), epistemic (obscuring knowledge construction), and relational (obscuring negotiations of agency and classroom authority). Analysis of the case illustrated how these black boxes opened through distance (children’s communication gaps), breakdown (AI errors), and innovation (negotiation over AI use), revealing hidden dynamics in AI integration, such as uncertainty, people at work, decisions, competition, and controversies. Teacher scaffolding emerged as a key mediator of child-AI interactions, translating children’s open-ended inquiries into AI-legible inputs, transforming AI errors into opportunities for evaluative judgement, and recalibrating children’s AI interactions into child-led scientific inquiry. Ultimately, the paper shows that the seamless integration of AI is neither realistic nor pedagogically effective, and exemplifies how emergent frictions can foster young learners’ AI literacy, evaluative judgement, and relational agency.

title: Community-based Screening for Autism Spectrum Disorder Among Children in Pondicherry: A Cross-sectional Study
journal: Journal of Indian Association for Child and Adolescent Mental Health
authors: Bhavani S, Sarah Catherine S, Nishanth Rajan, Priya Jose, Peter Prasanth Kumar K, Shanthi Kannan
abstract: Background: Most Indian studies on Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) are hospital-based, and community-level data using standardized screening tools remain limited. Community screening can help identify children at risk and generate hypotheses regarding associated factors. The main objective of the study was to screen for ASD among children in Pondicherry and to identify associated factors. Methods: A community-based cross-sectional screening study was conducted in rural and urban areas of Pondicherry between September 2023 and February 2024. Children aged 18 months to 14 years ( n = 272) were screened using the AIIMS-modified INCLEN diagnostic tool for ASD. Participants were recruited using convenience sampling. Socio-demographic details and information on perinatal, familial, environmental, and behavioral factors were collected through parental interviews. Environmental variables such as ventilation and overcrowding were self-reported. The proportion of screen-positive ASD was calculated. Associations between screen-positive ASD and various factors were explored using Fisher’s exact test and Mann–Whitney U test. Results: Seven children were found to be screen-positive for ASD, yielding a proportion of 2.57% (95% CI: 1.03%-5.26%) in this screened sample. Screen-positive ASD showed significant associations with male gender ( P = .006), age group 5–10 years ( P = .04), late preterm birth ( P = .013), respiratory distress at birth ( P = .015), and reduced time spent in outdoor play ( P = .033). Other socio-demographic, familial, and environmental variables did not show significant associations. These findings represent unadjusted exploratory associations. Conclusion: This community-based screening study identified a small proportion of children who screened positive for ASD and highlighted several factors that showed exploratory associations. The findings underscore the importance of community screening and the need for larger, methodologically robust studies to estimate the proportion and evaluate risk factors for ASD in the Indian context.

title: Multiscale Evaluation of Quercetin Against Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Vibrio vulnificus in Seafood and Food-Contact Surfaces
authors: Nigar Sultana Meghla, Md Furkanur Rahaman Mizan, Syeda Roufun Nesa, Sangha Han, Iksoon Kang, Sang-Do Ha
abstract: Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Vibrio vulnificus biofilms pose a major challenge to seafood safety owing to their persistence on food-contact surfaces and increased tolerance to antimicrobial interventions. This study investigated the antibiofilm efficacy and mechanisms of quercetin using integrated structural, physiological, and molecular approaches. Quercetin exhibited concentration-dependent biofilm inhibition and reduced mature biofilms on abiotic surfaces, while its efficacy in inhibiting biofilm formation was evaluated on seafood. Quercetin suppressed early biofilm establishment by reducing cell surface hydrophobicity, bacterial adhesion, autoaggregation, motility, cellular respiration, and ATP production, thereby limiting bacterial attachment and microcolony formation. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy revealed changes in the EPS-associated spectral profiles of both species, indicating alterations in the biochemical composition of the biofilm matrix. These spectral changes varied between V. vulnificus and V. parahaemolyticus. Gene expression analysis demonstrated coordinated downregulation of quorum sensing (QS), adhesion, and EPS biosynthesis genes, accompanied by increased membrane permeability, intracellular protein leakage, and metabolic dysfunction. In a 6 h screen, 1/2 MIC caused only minor changes in the color and texture of shrimp and oyster, whereas MIC caused larger changes; no cytotoxicity was detected under the tested conditions. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that quercetin disrupts Vibrio biofilms through coordinated mechanisms with limited short-term effects on seafood color and texture at 1/2 MIC, supporting further evaluation as a natural, industry-relevant strategy for controlling seafood-associated Vibrio biofilms and improving seafood safety.

title: A blended digital parenting intervention for the prevention of sexual violence, exploitative sex, and maltreatment of children at scale in Tanzania: a cluster-randomised, controlled trial.
authors: Cluver LD, Ornellas A, Klapwijk JM, Nyalali K, Chetty AN, Mgunga S, Melendez-Torres GJ, Kahwa J, Awah I, Baerecke L, Booij A, Christine L, de Graaf K, Lachman JM, Markle L, Mjwara SN, Stern D, Te Winkel E, Tsoanyane S, Sherr L, Wambura M, Green O, Ngcobo L, Mwakakeke S, Desmond C, Clements L, Kijoti E, Manjengenja N, Wamoyi J

title: Scaling guided play through educational media: bridging theory and practice across diverse global contexts
authors: Kim Foulds, Jennifer M. Zosh, Rosemarie Truglio, Jessica DiSalvo, Shanna Kohn, Autumn Zitani
abstract: This paper explores the intersection of theory and industry practice, examining how educational media leverages playful learning to facilitate transfer of learning in children living in diverse global contexts. Central to this discussion is the evolution of Sesame Street , highlighting its strategic shift toward utilizing guided play models. We ground this discussion in Esme &amp; Roy , an animated series that established Sesame Workshop's approach to modeling guided play on screen and show how that approach shaped two future productions: the playful “approaches to learning” curriculum of Sesame Street Seasons 51–52, and Watch, Play, Learn , a suite of early learning videos designed to support children affected by crisis and conflict. Together, these examples demonstrate how intentional media design can support transfer of learning across varied geographic contexts and how theory informs practice, which then further refines theory. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these advancements for the future of educational media and playful learning.

title: The Role of Parent–Child Relationships in Problematic Social Media Use and Mental Health among Chinese Adolescents
journal: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
authors: Yuxin Jiao
abstract: This study asked whether parent–child relationship quality helps explain the association of problematic social media use with self-esteem and depressive symptoms. A cross-sectional survey was completed by 115 high school students in China, aged 15–18. The questionnaire included the Mobile Phone Addiction Index and self-report measures of family relationships and mental health. Pearson correlations and two mediation models were estimated using PROCESS Model 4, one for each outcome. Students with higher problematic-use scores reported poorer parent–child relationships. Better relationship quality was associated with higher self-esteem, and the indirect estimate through relationship quality was significant for self-esteem. The corresponding estimate for depressive symptoms was not significant. The results support examining family relationships when considering adolescent self-esteem in the context of problematic use. They provide less support for the proposed indirect association with depressive symptoms. Measurements taken at a single time point cannot show whether problematic use precedes changes in family relationships or mental health.

title: English immersive game participation and attention, emotional health, and cognitive function in children: a cross-sectional study
authors: Jing Wu
abstract: Background Screen exposure is an important issue for children’s health. The existing research pays more attention to the duration of use, but not to the content type and immersion experience. English immersion game integrates language learning and game mechanism, which belongs to educational digital behavior. This study analyzes the daily English game duration, immersion and English integration of children aged 6–14, and their relationships with attention, working memory, executive function and emotional behavior. Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included 215 children. Based on the parents’ questionnaire, the data of English game participation were obtained: daily duration, 1–5 immersion self-evaluation, and English integration. The outcome includes all kinds of attention, working memory, executive function, emotion and ADHD symptoms. Multivariate linear regression controls total screen time, sleep, physical activity, age, gender and family SES. CPT, Flanker and Corsi were the main outcomes, and after Bonferroni correction, the four executive function and behavior indicators were set as exploratory outcomes, which were not corrected. Results English game time is positively correlated with selective attention ( β = 0.218, p = 0.001). It is significantly different from the primary analysis of working memory, and its effect size fell below the minimum-detectable-effect threshold following Bonferroni correction. Immersion self-rating is positively correlated with multiple attention and working memory, and negatively correlated with emotional symptoms. The degree of English integration is positively correlated with cognitive indicators and negatively correlated with emotional symptoms; After excluding the pure-English-immersion subgroup, the association with selective attention and inhibition control is no longer significant, and it is regarded as descriptive association. Daily screen time was negatively correlated with cognitive ability, and positively correlated with mood and ADHD symptoms (all p &lt; 0.001). Conclusion Different dimensions of English immersion games are related to children’s cognitive and emotional outcomes. In addition to the duration of use, the integration of game English is as important as the immersion experience. The results can provide reference for family digital activity selection, children’s screen behavior norms and campus digital education intervention, which still needs to be verified by longitudinal research.

title: English immersive game participation and attention, emotional health, and cognitive function in children: a cross-sectional study
authors: Jing Wu
abstract: Background Screen exposure is an important issue for children’s health. The existing research pays more attention to the duration of use, but not to the content type and immersion experience. English immersion game integrates language learning and game mechanism, which belongs to educational digital behavior. This study analyzes the daily English game duration, immersion and English integration of children aged 6–14, and their relationships with attention, working memory, executive function and emotional behavior. Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included 215 children. Based on the parents’ questionnaire, the data of English game participation were obtained: daily duration, 1–5 immersion self-evaluation, and English integration. The outcome includes all kinds of attention, working memory, executive function, emotion and ADHD symptoms. Multivariate linear regression controls total screen time, sleep, physical activity, age, gender and family SES. CPT, Flanker and Corsi were the main outcomes, and after Bonferroni correction, the four executive function and behavior indicators were set as exploratory outcomes, which were not corrected. Results English game time is positively correlated with selective attention ( β = 0.218, p = 0.001). It is significantly different from the primary analysis of working memory, and its effect size fell below the minimum-detectable-effect threshold following Bonferroni correction. Immersion self-rating is positively correlated with multiple attention and working memory, and negatively correlated with emotional symptoms. The degree of English integration is positively correlated with cognitive indicators and negatively correlated with emotional symptoms; After excluding the pure-English-immersion subgroup, the association with selective attention and inhibition control is no longer significant, and it is regarded as descriptive association. Daily screen time was negatively correlated with cognitive ability, and positively correlated with mood and ADHD symptoms (all p &lt; 0.001). Conclusion Different dimensions of English immersion games are related to children’s cognitive and emotional outcomes. In addition to the duration of use, the integration of game English is as important as the immersion experience. The results can provide reference for family digital activity selection, children’s screen behavior norms and campus digital education intervention, which still needs to be verified by longitudinal research.

title: Religious Communities and Social Media in North Macedonia: Between Digital Presence and Online Engagement
authors: Aleksandar Grizhev, Ivan Blazhevski, Ruzica Cacanoska
abstract: Religious communities increasingly operate within digital environments where institutional communication, religious practice, and audience interaction intersect. Yet, establishing a presence on social media does not necessarily translate into meaningful engagement or dialogue. This study examines how the principal religious communities in North Macedonia use social media platforms and how their institutional communication practices are reflected in the digital public sphere. Drawing on an exploratory qualitative content analysis conducted between January and June 2025, this research examines institutional and institutionally associated Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube accounts of the principal religious communities in the country while considering selected smaller communities where relevant. The analysis focuses on platform presence, posting practices, types of content, language use, multimedia formats, institutional organization, and patterns of interaction with followers. The findings reveal substantial differences in the visibility, intensity, and sophistication of digital communication across religious communities. However, despite greater use of multimedia, multilingual communication, and more frequent posting among some actors, communication remains predominantly oriented toward dissemination rather than sustained dialogue. More interactive practices are observed mainly in youth-oriented and community-focused accounts. This study argues that digital presence, dissemination, engagement, and dialogue should be understood as distinct but overlapping dimensions of institutional religious communication. It also contributes to the study of digital religion by examining these dynamics in a religiously plural Southeast European context.
